---
title: "Training Guide"
---


## Data format

Training data is stored as `.npy` files — pickled Python dicts with the following structure:

```python
{
    'data': ([img1, img2, ...], [mask1, mask2, ...]),  # images (YXC), masks (YX)
    'target': ['interphase', 'mitosis', ...]           # string class labels
}
```

The [Training Widget](../../napari/user-guide/training_widget.html) produces files in exactly
this format. Each file contains all annotations from one session (one plate / well / image
combination). Multiple files can coexist in the same directory and are combined by
`cellclass dataset`.

---

## Step 1 — Create dataset

::: {.callout-tip}
If you are working in Napari, this step is automated. Open the **Training Widget**, click
**Manage Sessions**, then **Export Dataset**. This runs `cellclass dataset` on all sessions
for the selected classifier and also writes a ready-to-use `train.txt` template — you can
skip straight to [Step 4](#step-4-generate-and-run-batchsh).
:::

To run manually from the command line:

```bash
cellclass dataset <data_dir> --name rois
```

What this does:

1. Globs all `*.npy` files in `<data_dir>`.
2. Drops any crop labelled `unassigned` (cells you reviewed but did not classify).
3. For each remaining crop: applies (1, 99) percentile stretch, centres the cell,
   and converts to `uint8`.
4. Deduplicates identical crops (by pixel hash) to avoid overfitting on repeated cells.
5. Writes `<data_dir>/rois.npz` — a single compressed numpy archive.

The `.npz` contains all crops in a single pool — train/validation/test splitting and
class imbalance handling are done by `cellclass train` at training time (see
[Step 4](#step-4-generate-and-run-batchsh)).

Channel names are read from `metadata.json` in the data directory. Override with `--channels`:

```bash
cellclass dataset ~/data/ppase_screen --channels DAPI RFP --name rois
```

Useful options:

| Flag | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `--name` | `rois` | Output filename stem |
| `--channels` | from metadata.json | Channel names (order must match image data) |
| `--ignore` | none | Class labels to exclude |
| `--size` | none | Resize all crops to `N×N` pixels |

---

## Step 2 — Sample and verify

Before training, visually verify your dataset:

```bash
cellclass sample ~/data/mitosis-rpe/rois.npz --output ~/data/mitosis-rpe
```

This writes one TIFF per class containing a random grid of crops in ImageJ hyperstack
format. Open in ImageJ with `Image → Color → Channels Tool → Composite` to check
channel assignments and label quality.

---

## Step 3 — Write `train.txt`

A batch file is a plain-text list of arguments for `cellclass train`, one run per line.
Comment lines (`#`) and blank lines are ignored. `cellclass batch` converts this file into
a `batch.sh` shell script, assigning unique checkpoint filenames automatically so runs
never overwrite each other.

---

### Flag reference

::: {.callout-note}
The authoritative, always-current list of options and defaults is the generated
[`cellclass train` reference](../reference/cli/train.html). The notes below add
the reasoning behind each flag — which value to pick, and why.
:::

#### Input

`dataset.npz` *(positional)*
: Path to the `.npz` file produced by `cellclass dataset`. You can also pass a `.json`
  state file to resume a crashed or paused run.

`--size N`
: Subsample `N` images randomly from the dataset. Default is all images. Useful for quick
  sanity checks (`--size 200`) without waiting for a full run.

`--data-seed INT` *(default: 42)*
: Random seed for subsampling. Change this to get a different random subset.

---

#### Model

`--model NAME` *(default: densenet121)*
: Neural network architecture. Available options:

  | Model | Size | Notes |
  |---|---|---|
  | `densenet121` | medium | Strong general-purpose performer |
  | `efficientnetb3s` | medium | ImageNet pretrained; use with `--freeze-weights` |
  | `shufflenet2x1_0` | light | Fast training, good baseline |
  | `squeezenet1_0` | lightest | Minimal memory; useful sanity check |

  See the [Model Guide](models.qmd) for full architecture details.

`--freeze-weights` / `--no-freeze-weights`
: Freeze the pretrained backbone and only train the classification head. Use this with
  `efficientnetb3s`, which ships with ImageNet weights. Freezing means the feature extractor
  is not updated — training is faster and needs less data, but the backbone cannot adapt to
  your specific channel content. For fluorescence images that look nothing like ImageNet
  photos, `--no-freeze-weights` often gives better final accuracy at the cost of slower
  convergence.

`--weights TEXT` *(default: DEFAULT)*
: PyTorch weights identifier. `DEFAULT` loads the standard pretrained weights for the
  chosen model. Pass `None` to start from a random initialisation (rarely needed — prefer
  `--no-freeze-weights` instead).

`--dropout FLOAT` *(default: 0.4)*
: Dropout rate applied to the final feature vector before the classification layer.
  Higher values (0.5–0.6) regularise more aggressively and help when the dataset is small
  or the feature vector is large. Lower values (0.2–0.3) suit larger datasets.

---

#### Learning rate

`--lr FLOAT` *(default: 1e-4)*
: Initial learning rate for the Adam optimiser. This is the single most important
  hyperparameter to sweep. Start with `1e-3` and `1e-4`; if both diverge, try `5e-4`.
  If both converge slowly, `1e-3` is usually better.

`--lr-scheduler TYPE` *(default: step)*
: How the learning rate decays during training.

  - **`plateau`** — reduces LR by `--lr-factor` when validation loss stops improving for
    `--lr-patience` epochs. Adapts to your data automatically. **Recommended for most runs.**
  - **`step`** — multiplies LR by `--lr-gamma` every `--lr-step` epochs regardless of
    performance. Predictable but requires more tuning.

`--lr-factor FLOAT` *(default: 0.1, plateau only)*
: Multiplicative factor applied when the plateau scheduler fires. `0.1` drops the LR by
  10×. Use `0.5` for a gentler reduction if training is unstable.

`--lr-patience INT` *(default: 2, plateau only)*
: Number of epochs with no improvement before the plateau scheduler fires. Increase to
  `5–10` if your loss curve is noisy.

`--lr-gamma FLOAT` *(default: 0.1, step only)*
: Multiplicative factor applied at each step. Same semantics as `--lr-factor` but for the
  step scheduler.

`--lr-step INT` *(default: 5, step only)*
: Epoch interval between step scheduler reductions.

`--weight-decay FLOAT` *(default: 1e-4)*
: L2 regularisation on model weights (Adam's `weight_decay`). Increase to `1e-3` if you
  see overfitting (training accuracy far above validation accuracy).

---

#### Training loop

`--epochs INT` *(default: 2000)*
: Maximum number of training epochs. Early stopping (controlled by `--patience`) usually
  terminates training well before this limit. Set lower (`--epochs 100`) for quick test
  runs on a laptop.

`--batch-size INT` *(default: 32)*
: Number of crops per gradient update. Larger batches train faster but require more GPU
  memory. Recommended values: `64` for medium models (DenseNet, EfficientNet), `128` for
  lightweight models (ShuffleNet, SqueezeNet).

`--patience INT` *(default: 10)*
: Early-stopping patience: training stops when validation accuracy has not improved for
  this many epochs. Increase to `20–30` for noisy datasets where improvement is slow.

`--delta FLOAT` *(default: 0)*
: Minimum *absolute* improvement in validation accuracy to reset the patience counter.
  Leave at `0` unless you want to ignore very small improvements.

`--rel-delta FLOAT` *(default: 1e-4)*
: Minimum *relative* improvement (as a fraction of current accuracy) to count as
  progress. Prevents tiny numerical fluctuations from resetting the patience counter.

`--validation-size FLOAT` *(default: 0.2)*
: Fraction of data held out for validation during training. The remaining `1 - validation-size - testing-size` fraction is used for training.

`--seed INT` *(default: 0xDEADBEEF)*
: Random seed for model initialisation and data splits. Fix this across runs when you want
  to isolate the effect of a single hyperparameter change.

---

#### Loss function

`--loss-function TYPE` *(default: focal_loss)*
: Loss function used during training.

  - **`focal_loss`** — down-weights easy examples so the model focuses on hard or rare
    cases. **Recommended for imbalanced datasets** (e.g. many interphase cells, few mitotic).
  - **`cross_entropy`** — standard classification loss. Use when classes are balanced.

`--focal-gamma FLOAT` *(default: 2)*
: Focusing parameter for focal loss. Higher values (3–5) concentrate training even more on
  hard examples. Effective range is 0.5–5; `2` is the standard from the original paper.

`--loss-weights` / `--no-loss-weights`
: Weight each class in the loss by the inverse of its frequency. Helps with imbalanced
  datasets independently of focal loss — you can combine both. Disabled by default.

---

#### Data augmentation

`--flip INT` *(default: 1)*
: Random flip augmentation applied each epoch.

  | Value | Effect |
  |---|---|
  | `0` | No flipping |
  | `1` | Horizontal flips only |
  | `2` | Vertical flips only |
  | `3` | Both horizontal and vertical |

  Use `3` for cell images — cells have no preferred orientation.

`--rotate INT` *(default: 180)*
: Maximum rotation angle in degrees. Each crop is randomly rotated by ±`rotate` degrees.
  `180` means full random rotation, which is appropriate for round objects like cells.
  Set to `0` to disable.

`--translate FLOAT` *(default: 0.1)*
: Maximum translation as a fraction of image size. `0.1` shifts crops by up to 10% in
  each direction. Helps the model generalise to slightly off-centre cells.

---

#### Hardware

`-d DEVICE` *(default: cuda)*
: Compute device.

  | Value | When to use |
  |---|---|
  | `cuda` | NVIDIA GPU (Linux/Windows server) |
  | `cuda:0`, `cuda:1` | Specific GPU on a multi-GPU machine |
  | `mps` | Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3 Mac) |
  | `cpu` | Fallback; very slow for anything but tiny tests |

`--num-workers INT` *(default: 0)*
: Number of parallel workers for data loading. On Linux with CUDA, `4` or `8` significantly
  reduces data loading bottlenecks. **Set to `0` on macOS** (MPS does not support forked
  workers).

`--cudnn-benchmark`
: Enables cuDNN autotuning — benchmarks convolution algorithms at startup and picks the
  fastest one for your specific input size. Adds ~30 s startup overhead but speeds up
  training. **CUDA only; omit on MPS/CPU.**

`--pin-memory`
: Uses CUDA pinned (page-locked) memory in the DataLoader for faster host→GPU transfers.
  **CUDA only; omit on MPS/CPU.**

---

#### Testing

`--testing-size FLOAT` *(default: 0.2)*
: Fraction of data held out as a final test set, evaluated once at the end of training.
  This split is never seen during training or validation.

`--testing-interval INT` *(default: 5)*
: Evaluate the held-out test set every N epochs (in addition to the final evaluation).
  Useful for monitoring generalisation during training; set higher to reduce overhead.

---

#### Weights & Biases

`--wandb`
: Enable logging to Weights & Biases. Requires a prior `wandb login`. Runs are logged to
  the `cellclass` project in your own workspace by default.

`--entity TEXT`
: W&B team or username. Defaults to your logged-in account. Pass `--entity myteam` to log
  to a shared team project.

`--project TEXT` *(default: cellclass)*
: W&B project name.

`--run-name TEXT`
: Human-readable display name for this run in the W&B UI. If not set, W&B generates one.

`--tags TAG [TAG ...]`
: One or more tags attached to the run, useful for filtering in W&B. Example:
  `--tags mitosis rpe 50px`.

---

### Standard sweep (GPU server)

The default sweep covers four architectures and two learning rates — six runs total.
This is a good starting point for any new dataset.

```text
rois.npz --model efficientnetb3s --freeze-weights --lr 1e-3 --lr-scheduler plateau --flip 3 --batch-size 64 -d cuda --cudnn-benchmark --pin-memory --num-workers 4 --wandb
rois.npz --model efficientnetb3s --freeze-weights --lr 1e-4 --lr-scheduler plateau --flip 3 --batch-size 64 -d cuda --cudnn-benchmark --pin-memory --num-workers 4 --wandb
rois.npz --model densenet121 --lr 1e-3 --lr-scheduler plateau --flip 3 --batch-size 64 -d cuda --cudnn-benchmark --pin-memory --num-workers 4 --wandb
rois.npz --model densenet121 --lr 1e-4 --lr-scheduler plateau --flip 3 --batch-size 64 -d cuda --cudnn-benchmark --pin-memory --num-workers 4 --wandb
rois.npz --model shufflenet2x1_0 --lr 1e-3 --lr-scheduler plateau --flip 3 --batch-size 128 -d cuda --cudnn-benchmark --pin-memory --num-workers 4 --wandb
rois.npz --model squeezenet1_0 --lr 1e-3 --lr-scheduler plateau --flip 3 --batch-size 128 -d cuda --cudnn-benchmark --pin-memory --num-workers 4 --wandb
```

### Quick test on Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3)

Use a single lightweight model with reduced epochs to verify everything works before
sending to the GPU server. MPS does not support `--cudnn-benchmark`, `--pin-memory`,
or `--num-workers > 0`.

```text
rois.npz --model shufflenet2x1_0 --lr 1e-3 --lr-scheduler plateau --flip 3 --batch-size 32 -d mps --num-workers 0 --epochs 50
```

### Small or imbalanced dataset

When you have fewer than ~500 annotated cells per class, or a large class imbalance
(e.g. 10× more interphase than mitotic cells), combine focal loss with loss weights and
increase regularisation:

```text
rois.npz --model shufflenet2x1_0 --lr 1e-3 --lr-scheduler plateau --lr-patience 5 --flip 3 --rotate 180 --batch-size 64 -d cuda --loss-function focal_loss --focal-gamma 3 --loss-weights --dropout 0.5 --patience 20 --wandb
rois.npz --model densenet121 --lr 1e-4 --lr-scheduler plateau --lr-patience 5 --flip 3 --rotate 180 --batch-size 32 -d cuda --loss-function focal_loss --focal-gamma 3 --loss-weights --dropout 0.5 --patience 20 --wandb
```

### Unfreezing EfficientNet

By default `--freeze-weights` only trains the classification head. If accuracy plateaus,
add a second run without freezing to let the backbone adapt to fluorescence images:

```text
# Phase 1: fast convergence with frozen backbone
rois.npz --model efficientnetb3s --freeze-weights --lr 1e-3 --lr-scheduler plateau --flip 3 --batch-size 64 -d cuda --wandb --run-name effnet-frozen
# Phase 2: fine-tune full network at lower LR
rois.npz --model efficientnetb3s --no-freeze-weights --lr 1e-4 --lr-scheduler plateau --flip 3 --batch-size 64 -d cuda --wandb --run-name effnet-finetune
```

---

## Step 4 — Generate and run `batch.sh`

```bash
cellclass batch train.txt --script batch.sh
bash batch.sh
```

`cellclass batch` assigns unique checkpoint and metadata filenames automatically so runs
never overwrite each other. Comment out completed lines in `train.txt` before regenerating.

To run jobs in parallel (one per GPU on a multi-GPU machine):

```bash
cellclass batch train.txt --script batch.sh --background
bash batch.sh
```

Each run launches as a background process; add `--device cuda:0`, `cuda:1`, etc. per line
to assign GPUs explicitly.

### Data splits

The `.npz` is split into three non-overlapping sets at the start of each training run:

- **64 %** training
- **16 %** validation — monitored each epoch for early stopping
- **20 %** held-out test set — evaluated once at the end, never seen during training

These come from the defaults `--testing-size 0.2` and `--validation-size 0.2` (validation
is 20 % of the remaining 80 %). For small datasets try `--testing-size 0.1
--validation-size 0.1` to get an 80/10/10 split.

::: {.callout-warning}
The test split is **not saved to disk** — it is reconstructed at evaluation time by
replaying the same random split using `--data-seed`. The split is therefore only
genuinely held-out if you use **the same `.npz` and the same seed** as training. The
`.json` state file records the seed used, so always pass it to `cellclass test`:

```bash
cellclass test rois.npz.1.json --data-seed 42
```

If you add new annotations and regenerate `rois.npz`, the crop indices shift and the old
split no longer applies — the model may be tested on cells it trained on. Only regenerate
`rois.npz` when you intend to retrain from scratch.
:::

### Class imbalance

Imbalance is handled in the loss function, not by resampling:

- **Focal loss** (default) down-weights easy, correctly-classified examples so training
  concentrates on hard or rare cases. This handles moderate imbalance well on its own.
- **`--loss-weights`** additionally scales each class's loss contribution by its inverse
  frequency. Combine with focal loss when one class is 5× or more rarer than another.

The splits are not stratified, so with very small datasets (<50 cells per class) the test
set may by chance contain an unrepresentative ratio. Check per-class counts in the W&B
logs and fix `--data-seed` if this is a concern.

---

## Step 5 — Compare on Weights & Biases

Open your W&B dashboard at <https://wandb.ai> and navigate to the **cellclass** project in your workspace. The key metrics to compare:

- **val/acc** — validation accuracy (primary metric for model selection).
- **test/acc** — held-out test accuracy (reported at end of training).
- **val/loss** — validation loss curve (check for overfitting).

Download the best run's metadata JSON from the W&B artifacts panel, or find it locally
in your working directory.

---

## Step 6 — Extract the model

```bash
cellclass extract best_run.json
```

Without `--save` this prints the performance metrics without writing any files — useful
for a quick sanity check. Add `--save` to export:

```bash
cellclass extract best_run.json --save
```

Output files:

- `<model>_c<channels>_l<labels>.pt` — TorchScript model.
- `<model>_c<channels>_l<labels>.json` — sidecar metadata (channels, labels, image size).

---

## Step 7 — Test the exported model

```bash
cellclass test -s shufflenet2x1_0_c2_l2.pt ~/data/mitosis-rpe/rois.npz
```

Prints a per-class precision/recall/F1 report and overall accuracy on the test split.

---

## Resuming a crashed run

Training checkpoints are saved after each epoch. To restart from the last checkpoint:

```bash
cellclass train best_run.json
```

Passing the metadata JSON resumes from the saved checkpoint. Note: some training state
(e.g. convergence checker) is not persisted and is recreated from scratch.
